patient.name: Chloe Mensah
patient.complaint: Cough for 10 days after a cold, now bringing up green sputum
background: Had a runny nose and sore throat two weeks ago
No asthma, COPD, diabetes or heart disease
Works in a busy call centre in Croydon

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with cough after a cold, mild fever and wheeze or rhonchi but **no focal consolidation**: the chest signs separate bronchitis from pneumonia.

points: It started after a cold two weeks ago.
Now green sputum, a tight chest, some wheeze.
She still feels well enough to work.

steps.lead: Chloe's cough after a cold points to a **viral** infection of the bronchi, not the alveoli.
Her recent **URTI** and **smoking** are the two classic risk factors; rhinovirus is the likeliest culprit.

points: Chest: scattered **rhonchi that clear after coughing**.
No bronchial breathing, no dullness, no focal crackles.

steps.lead: Green sputum does **not** mean bacteria. What matters is the absence of **focal consolidation signs**.

steps.q: Chloe has rhonchi clearing on coughing and no focal signs. What is it?
steps.r: Cough after a URTI with **no focal signs** is acute bronchitis. Focal crackles or bronchial breathing would suggest pneumonia.

steps.title: Acute bronchitis vs pneumonia vs asthma
head: Feature
Acute bronchitis
Pneumonia

steps.lead: Chloe is safety-netted: **high fever, breathlessness or chest pain** would mean progression to pneumonia.

steps.text: Sputum colour is a poor guide. Green or yellow sputum is common in **viral** bronchitis and does not justify antibiotics.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical diagnosis), or a chest X-ray when pneumonia cannot be excluded.

steps.q: Chloe asks for tests to 'find the bug'. What confirms her diagnosis?
steps.r: Acute bronchitis is a **clinical diagnosis**. Tests would not change her management.

steps.lead: Chloe's history and chest examination are the test: **no routine investigations** needed.

steps.text: Investigations are for **doubt**: when focal signs, high fever or hypoxia make pneumonia possible.

steps.title: Point-of-care CRP (practice nurse)
steps.text: A mildly raised CRP fits a viral bronchitis; the key cut-off for antibiotics is 100 mg/L.

steps.lead: Had Chloe's chest signs been uncertain, a **chest X-ray** would be used to exclude pneumonia.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Clear lung fields, no consolidation, no effusion: **pneumonia excluded**.

steps.text: This is what a CXR would show in bronchitis: normal. Consolidation would change the diagnosis.
Do not send sputum culture or bloods routinely. They add cost and delay and do not alter the plan.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': self-care and analgesia for most, salbutamol only with airway disease, and doxycycline for 5 days only in high-risk patients (comorbidity, age over 80, CRP over 100).

steps.q: Chloe is well, 36, no comorbidities, CRP 22. What does she need?
steps.r: Most cases need **reassurance and self-care**. She has none of the high-risk features for antibiotics.

steps.lead: Chloe gets **reassurance**, fluids, **paracetamol or ibuprofen**, and stop-smoking advice. No inhaler: she has no underlying airway disease.

steps.title: Who gets what
nodes: Cough after URTI, no focal signs
High risk: comorbidity, age >80 or CRP >100

steps.lead: If Chloe had **heart failure or diabetes**, were **over 80**, or had a **CRP over 100**, she would get **doxycycline for 5 days**.
Chloe's plan follows **NICE NG120** on acute cough: no antibiotic for most, targeted antibiotics for high risk.

steps.text: A short-acting bronchodilator is not for everyone with wheeze: the notes say **only if underlying airway disease** such as asthma.
Tell Chloe the cough may last **3 to 4 weeks**. Expecting it reduces repeat visits for antibiotics.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the most likely organism (rhinovirus), why the chest has no consolidation, why cough lasts weeks, and why antibiotics rarely help.

steps.lead: Chloe's virus infected her **tracheobronchial epithelium**: inflamed airways and extra mucus, but her alveoli stayed clear.
Chloe's cough will outlast the virus because the airway lining stays **inflamed and hyperresponsive** for weeks.

visual.title: Chloe's cough over time
visual.caption: Fever settles in days but the cough lingers **for weeks**: airway inflammation outlasts the virus.

steps.q: Why will antibiotics not help Chloe?
o: The drugs cannot reach the bronchi
steps.r: Acute bronchitis is almost always **viral**, so antibiotics offer little benefit and add side effects and resistance.

steps.lead: Antibiotics are saved for those where **bacterial superinfection** is more likely or more dangerous.

steps.text: **Rhinovirus** is the most common cause; influenza, coronavirus and RSV are others.

technique.stem: A 42 year old man has had a cough for 2 weeks, productive of green sputum. It began after a cold. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. There are scattered rhonchi that clear after coughing, and no focal signs.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about cough: bronchi or alveoli?
Post-URTI cough, smoker, rhonchi clearing on cough, **no focal signs**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute bronchitis.

elim: No history of episodic wheeze or atopy; this followed a cold.
Pneumonia gives **focal** signs; there are none.
No COPD diagnosis and he is only 42.
Two weeks after a cold is too short; no weight loss or haemoptysis.

steps.x: **A. Acute bronchitis.** Rule: cough after URTI + no focal signs = acute bronchitis; green sputum does not change it.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman has had a cough with clear sputum for 8 days after a sore throat. She feels otherwise well. Classic, well, normal sats, no focal signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical diagnosis: no tests.

elim: Only if pneumonia cannot be excluded; she has no focal signs.
Would not change management.
For suspected asthma or COPD, not an acute viral cough.
Not needed: the cause is almost always viral.

steps.x: **C. No investigation required.** Rule: typical acute bronchitis is a **clinical diagnosis**.

technique.stem: An 84 year old woman has had a cough productive of yellow sputum for 9 days after a cold. She lives independently. Not the antibiotic or duration the notes give.

technique.stem: A 25 year old man has acute bronchitis after a cold. His temperature is 37.5°C. He is worried because his cough is still present 3 weeks later, although his fever settled after 2 days.

steps.x: Prolonged airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.

The virus has usually cleared; the airway is still inflamed.

steps.x: **D. Ongoing airway epithelial inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.** Rule: bronchitis cough lasts **weeks** after the virus clears.

glossary.acute bronchitis: Short-lived, usually viral, inflammation of the bronchi causing cough, without lung consolidation.
glossary.bronchi: The large airways branching from the trachea into each lung.
glossary.tracheobronchial: Relating to the trachea and bronchi together.
glossary.rhinovirus: The common cold virus; the most common cause of acute bronchitis.
glossary.RSV: Respiratory syncytial virus; a common respiratory virus, worst in infants and the elderly.
glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection, such as a cold or sore throat.
glossary.rhonchi: Low-pitched rattling sounds from mucus in large airways, often clearing after a cough.
glossary.wheeze: High-pitched whistling from narrowed airways, usually on breathing out.
glossary.end-expiratory: Occurring at the end of breathing out.
glossary.consolidation: Alveoli filled with fluid or pus, as in pneumonia; gives focal signs and CXR shadowing.
glossary.focal signs: Chest signs in one area, such as crackles, dullness or bronchial breathing, suggesting consolidation.
glossary.bronchial breathing: Harsh, hollow breath sounds heard over consolidated lung.
glossary.alveoli: Tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens.
glossary.pneumonia: Infection of the lung tissue with alveolar consolidation.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; a blood marker of inflammation used to guide antibiotics in acute cough.
glossary.point-of-care: A test done at the bedside or in the surgery with a result within minutes.
glossary.doxycycline: Tetracycline antibiotic; first-line for acute bronchitis when antibiotics are indicated.
glossary.salbutamol: Short-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler that opens narrowed airways.
glossary.bronchodilator: A drug that widens the airways, such as salbutamol.
glossary.hyperresponsiveness: Airways that narrow too easily in response to triggers.
glossary.mucociliary clearance: Hair-like cilia sweeping mucus out of the airways.
glossary.superinfection: A second, often bacterial, infection on top of a first, often viral, one.
glossary.NG120: NICE guideline on antimicrobial prescribing for acute cough.
glossary.safety-netting: Telling a patient which warning signs should prompt them to return.
glossary.comorbidity: Another long-term condition the patient has, such as diabetes or heart failure.
glossary.pertussis: Whooping cough, caused by Bordetella pertussis, with paroxysmal coughing fits.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: fixed airflow obstruction, usually from smoking.
glossary.antimicrobial stewardship: Using antibiotics only when needed to limit resistance and side effects.
